```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(transmap)
data(transmap_example)
data_list <- list(Z = transmap_example$z, N = transmap_example$n)
```

A global program is a sparse set of genes jointly associated with a sparse set
of *trans* variants. `r_transcca()` finds programs by a sparse rank-$K$
decomposition of the variants $\times$ genes matrix $W$ (see
[Constructing the W Matrix](Constructing_W_Matrix.html)).

# 1. The transCCA model

With genotypes $G$ and expression $E$, the leading pair of canonical
variables for variants ($u$) and genes ($v$) solves

$$(u, v) = \arg\max_{u, v} \; u^\top G^\top E \, v = \arg\max_{u, v} \; u^\top W v.$$

transCCA adds sparsity by penalized matrix decomposition (PMD; Witten et al.,
2009):

$$\max_{u, v} \; u^\top W v \quad \text{subject to} \quad
\|u\|_2 \le 1, \; \|v\|_2 \le 1, \;
\|u\|_1 \le c_u, \; \|v\|_1 \le c_v.$$

The $L_1$ bounds are $c_u = \text{sumabs} \cdot \sqrt{P}$ and
$c_v = \text{sumabs} \cdot \sqrt{G}$ for $P$ variants and $G$ genes, so a
smaller `sumabs` gives sparser programs. After each program, $W$ is deflated,
$W \leftarrow W - d_k u_k v_k^\top$, and the next program is fitted. Each
program $k$ has

- gene loadings $v_k$ (column $k$ of `V`): which genes are in the program;
- variant loadings $u_k$ (column $k$ of `U`): which variants affect it;
- a strength $d_k = u_k^\top W v_k$, reported as `d2_score` $= d_k^2$.

# 2. Fit transCCA

The example data has two simulated programs: variants 1-10 affect
`GENE01`-`GENE12`, and variants 11-20 affect `GENE25`-`GENE36` and
`GENE40`-`GENE45`.

```{r fit}
prog <- r_transcca(data_list, K = 2, sumabs = 0.25)
names(prog)
prog$d2_score
```

### Variant loadings

```{r variants}
lapply(seq_len(ncol(prog$U)), function(k) {
  which(prog$U[, k] != 0)
})
```

Both sets of causal variants are recovered exactly, each by its own program.

### Gene loadings

```{r genes}
lapply(seq_len(ncol(prog$V)), function(k) {
  v <- prog$V[, k]
  v <- v[v != 0]
  round(v[order(-abs(v))], 3)
})
```

All selected genes belong to the simulated programs. At this sparsity level
only the genes with the strongest associations are kept; a larger `sumabs`
keeps more genes (Section 4).

The sign of a program is arbitrary: $u_k$ and $v_k$ can flip sign together
without changing $d_k$. Here program 1 has positive variant loadings and
negative gene loadings, consistent with the negative simulated effects of
variants 11-20. Interpret loadings by their magnitude and by the sign of $u_k$
relative to $v_k$.

# 3. Choosing the number of programs `K`

When `K = NULL` (the default), `K` is chosen from the singular values of $W$:

- `select_method = "max"` (default): the largest gap between consecutive
  singular values;
- `select_method = "var_explain"`: the smallest number whose cumulative
  singular values exceed a fraction `var_exp` of the total.

```{r singular, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 3.5}
s <- prog$singular_values
plot(s[1:15], type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "Index",
     ylab = "Singular value of W")
which.max(-diff(s))
```

The largest gap follows the second singular value, matching the two simulated
programs. `select_style = "eigen"` computes the values from the eigen
decomposition of $W^\top W$ (or $W W^\top$) instead of the SVD.

# 4. Choosing the sparsity `sumabs`

Smaller `sumabs` gives sparser programs:

```{r sparsity}
sparsity <- t(sapply(c(0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.4), function(s) {
  fit <- r_transcca(data_list, K = 2, sumabs = s)
  c(sumabs = s, genes = colSums(fit$V != 0), variants = colSums(fit$U != 0))
}))
sparsity
```

When `sumabs = NULL` (the default), it is chosen by cross-validation with
`PMA::PMD.cv()` over a grid from $\max(1/\sqrt{P}, 1/\sqrt{G}) + 0.01$ to 0.8.
Cross-validation is random, so set a seed:

```{r cv}
set.seed(1)
prog_cv <- r_transcca(data_list)
prog_cv$sparsity
ncol(prog_cv$V)
colSums(prog_cv$V != 0)
```

Cross-validation optimizes the reconstruction of $W$ and tends to favour denser
programs than a fixed small `sumabs`. Choose a fixed `sumabs` when
interpretable, sparse programs are the goal, and check the selected genes and
variants.

### A separate sparsity per program

With `different_sparsity = TRUE`, the sparsity is re-tuned by cross-validation
for every program on the deflated matrix. Programs whose tuned sparsity falls
to the lower bound are set to zero, which acts as a stopping rule:

```{r diff-sparsity}
set.seed(1)
prog_diff <- r_transcca(data_list, K = 3, different_sparsity = TRUE)
round(prog_diff$sparsity, 3)
round(prog_diff$d2_score, 3)
```

# 5. Other options

- `normalization`: scale of `d2_score`. `"original"` (default) uses $W$ as is;
  `"F_norm"` divides $W$ by its squared Frobenius norm; `"max"` divides by its
  largest absolute entry. Use the same choice for observed and null fits.
- `null_thres`: if the largest absolute entry of $W$ is below this value, no
  program is fitted and `V`, `U`, `d` and `d2_score` are `NULL`.
- `exclude`, `tol`, `sig_cut`: passed to `w_construction()`, e.g. to mask
  *cis* pairs.
- `...`: further arguments to `PMA::PMD()` when `different_sparsity = FALSE`.

```{r exclude}
variant_chr <- rep(c("chr1", "chr2", "chr3"), each = 50)
gene_chr <- rep(c("chr1", "chr2", "chr3"), length.out = 60)
cis <- outer(variant_chr, gene_chr, "==")
prog_trans <- r_transcca(data_list, K = 2, sumabs = 0.25, exclude = cis)
prog_trans$d2_score
```

# 6. Other input types

Any `data_list` accepted by `w_construction()` works the same way. For example,
individual-level data whitened by the in-sample expression covariance:

```{r individual}
set.seed(2)
G <- scale(matrix(rbinom(300 * 20, 2, 0.3), 300, 20,
                  dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("rs", 1:20))))
E <- transmap_example$Y[, 1:30]
E[, 1:12] <- E[, 1:12] + G[, 1]
prog_ind <- r_transcca(list(G = G, E = scale(E), Sigma_EE = "insample"),
                       K = 1, sumabs = 0.4)
prog_ind$input
head(sort(abs(prog_ind$U[, 1]), decreasing = TRUE), 3)
```

The variant with the simulated effect, `rs1`, has the largest loading.

Continue with [Null Testing of Global Programs](Global_Program_Null_Testing.html).

# Reference

Witten DM, Tibshirani R, Hastie T (2009). A penalized matrix decomposition,
with applications to sparse principal components and canonical correlation
analysis. *Biostatistics* 10(3):515-534.
